name: Rafael Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm goes at a quarter to five, and I'm in the parlour at Hollin Farm by half five. Gwen Marsh owns the place, about 180 dairy cows plus barley and grass for silage. I do the morning milking with Kofi, scrape the yards, feed the calves, and in summer I'm on the old tractor carting silage. I've only been at it four years, so Gwen still won't let me near the combine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Four years. What were you doing before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-six years at the Brayford paper mill, on the rewinders, until they shut it in 2021. I was shop steward there for the last ten. When the mill went I was 53, and nobody wanted a 53-year-old paper man, so I asked around and Gwen took me on at the bottom. It's honest work and I like the cows, but my knees tell me every morning that I started late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the calves, and I like the quiet in the parlour before the radio goes on. What wears me out is the cold and the hours, and the feeling that I'm always the one learning while lads half my age know it already. Ines, my partner, cooks at the primary school, and between us we get by. We've maybe four months put by, and my mill pension is small, so I need to keep going till the state pension at 67.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the machines were never the problem, it's who owns them. If it's mostly hype, then fine, the cows still need milking and Gwen still needs hands. Online I don't do much, but at the union branch I'd tell them not to relax, because the squeeze on farmworkers doesn't need robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays about the same, and the same isn't easy. Milk price goes up and down, Gwen talks about selling every bad year, and I'm the newest one here. If Hollin Farm sold up, I'd be a 58-year-old milker with four years' experience looking for a yard that wants me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and keep my head down, same as now. I'd try to put another fifty a month into the savings, so we get to six months by the time I'm 60. And I'd ask Gwen straight out, over tea after milking, whether she's still thinking of selling, because I'd rather know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly, and a bit uneasy. It's not AI that keeps me awake, it's my knees and the milk cheque. I know what it's like to see a workplace shut, and that never really leaves you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Gwen talks about selling. How real is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every spring when the milk price drops she says she's had enough. Her son works in an office in the city and doesn't want the farm. I think she'll keep going five more years, maybe, but I've been wrong before. I thought the paper mill would outlast me too, and now I'm a 58-year-old learning to milk cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what would you want to be doing at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still milking, if my knees hold, then maybe just the calves part-time. Ines wants us to have one proper holiday before we're too old. I'd settle for keeping the job, the house warm and the grandkids visiting on Sundays.

say: The **machines** were never the problem; the question is always **who owns them**.
Farmworkers are **squeezed already**, so the union shouldn't relax just because AI turned out to be hype.
think: Life stays the same, and the same means a **milk price** that swings and an owner who talks of selling.
As the **newest hand** at 58, I'd struggle to find another yard if Hollin Farm sold.
do: Keep turning up for **half five milking** and keep my head down at Hollin Farm.
Add about **fifty a month** to savings, aiming for six months' cover by 60.
Ask Gwen **straight out** over tea whether she's still thinking of selling the herd.
feel: **Tired** and a little uneasy, more about my knees and the milk cheque than about AI.
S0.quote: I thought the paper mill would outlast me too, and now I'm a 58-year-old learning to milk cows.
fieldNote: The **mill closure** in 2021 colours everything; he reads every workplace as something that can shut.
His worry is **ownership and pay**, not technology; he frames it like a shop steward.
The real risk he names is **Gwen selling**, which exists with or without AI.

steps.text: Keep doing the half-five milking at Hollin Farm
Put another 50 a month into savings towards six months' cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the branch meeting that this is exactly when you need a union, before the change, not after. The office side of farming goes first: the feed ordering, the milk records, the vet bookings. On the yard I'd tell Kofi that the robots are slow coming, so we've got time to fight for proper terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Gwen would look harder at a milking robot. They exist already, those box robots the cows walk into by themselves, and if AI makes the paperwork cheaper she might put the savings towards one. Milking is most of what I do, so that's my hours, not someone else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd get Gwen to tell us her plans in writing, through the union if needed. I'd push the branch for an agreement on retraining and notice for farm staff. And I'd stop the holiday fund and put it into savings, because if they cut me to part-time I'd need to cover the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'd say. I'm not panicking, because it's slow and I can see it coming. But I've watched a rewinder line get replaced, and I learned something there. Bosses always say a new machine will come in gradually, right up until the morning it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Gwen did buy a milking robot, what would you say to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask her who's going to fix it at two in the morning when it throws an alarm, and whether that's going to be me on a call-out rate. I wouldn't fight the machine itself; I'd fight being thrown off without notice. Gwen's fair, mostly, so I think she'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I've no interest. Tomas, my son, keeps showing me the chat thing on his phone and I just hand it back. If Gwen wants the records done by a computer, let the computer do it; I'll do the cows.

say: This is the moment you need a **union**: before the change arrives, not after the jobs are gone.
Farm **paperwork** goes first, and robots on the yard are slow, so there's time to win **proper terms**.
think: Cheaper paperwork could free money for a **milking robot**, and milking is most of my hours.
Owners always say change will be **gradual** until suddenly it isn't, just like at the mill.
do: Ask Gwen to put her **plans in writing**, with the union's help if she won't.
Push the branch for a **farm-staff agreement** on notice periods and retraining.
Move the **holiday fund** into savings in case my hours are cut to part-time.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicking, because the slow pace gives me time to see it coming.
**Bitter** memories of the mill make me distrust promises of a gentle change.
S1.quote: Bosses always say a new machine will come in gradually, right up until the morning it doesn't.
fieldNote: He jumps straight to the **milking robot**, which already exists, so his fear is concrete and close.
He wants **collective protection** rather than a personal plan; he won't touch AI tools himself.
Moving the **holiday fund** shows the worry is real even though he speaks calmly.

steps.text: Ask Gwen through the union for her robot plans in writing
Push the branch for notice and retraining terms for farm staff
Move the holiday fund into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster that nobody planned for, and it's the government's job to make sure the gains don't all go to the owners. At the branch I'd say we need a jobs guarantee or a decent bridge to pension for older workers. Online I'd probably share the union's posts and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm finished by 2031. I'll be 63, four years short of the state pension, and the robot milks better than me and doesn't need its knees. The thinking part comes first in 2028, and Gwen would be told by some AI adviser exactly how many hands she can drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd write to our MP with the branch, asking for an early pension bridge for farmworkers over 60. I'd save every spare penny, maybe two hundred a month by cutting the car and the takeaway on Fridays. And I'd talk to Sofia and Tomas about whether we might need help, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's a good word for it. It's the mill all over again, but this time there's no next job to go to, because the robots will be on every farm at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in those three years between the thinking AI and the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The years between the thinking AI and the farm robots would be a waiting room where I'd still be milking but know my last day. That's almost worse than a surprise. I'd use it to fight for the pension bridge, because once the robots come there's no bargaining power left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate asking your children for help. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm supposed to be helping them. Sofia's a nurse with two little ones and a big rent. Asking my daughter for money at 63 would feel like the mill closing twice.

say: Nobody **planned** for this, and government must stop the gains going **only to owners**.
Older farmworkers need a **jobs guarantee** or a proper bridge to their pension.
think: By **2031** I'm 63 and replaced, four years short of the state pension.
In 2028 an **AI adviser** would tell Gwen exactly how many hands she can drop.
do: Write to our **MP** with the branch, asking for an early pension bridge for older farmworkers.
Save **two hundred a month** by cutting the second car and the Friday takeaway.
Talk to **Sofia and Tomas** about family help, though I'd hate to ask.
feel: **Alarmed**, because it feels like the mill closing with no next job anywhere.
**Ashamed** at the thought of asking my children for money.
S2.quote: The years between the thinking AI and the farm robots would be a waiting room where I'd still be milking but know my last day.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** as the only window for bargaining, not as breathing room.
His plan is **political and collective**; the personal side is mostly cutting and saving.
Pride shows when he talks about **asking his daughter** for money.

steps.text: Write to the MP with the branch about a pension bridge
Join union pressure for a farmworker jobs guarantee
Sell the second car and stop Friday takeaways to save 200 monthly
Ask Sofia and Tomas whether they could help us out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but with more time to organise. I'd say the five years should be used to write the rules now: who pays for the transition, what happens to people like me. I'd tell anyone who'd listen that waiting until 2031 is waiting too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots come in 2034 and I'm 66 then, so I'd be scraping into the state pension a year early. It's tight but it's nearly the finish line. The thinking AI in 2031 might still push Gwen to cut hours before that, so the last few years could be thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep milking and keep saving, maybe a hundred a month more, to cover a year of reduced hours. I'd go to the branch's campaign meetings on the transition fund and vote for whoever backs it. And I'd ask Gwen whether I could stay on part-time with the calves till 67.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still, but it's not the same panic. It's like seeing the bus pull away but knowing the next one comes in time if you run. I'd be tired, though, running for it at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your wife Ines works at a school. Does any of this touch her job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines's job is cooking for kids, and I can't see a robot doing that by 2031 in a primary school kitchen. Her pay keeps us steady if mine dips. That's a comfort, honestly, more than anything the government might do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're nearly at the finish line. Does that make you less angry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less scared, not less angry. I'll get out just about, but the young lads like Kofi won't. Our young farmhand Kofi is 24, and a robot would take his whole working life before he turns 32.

say: Use the **five years** to write the rules now: who pays for the transition and who is protected.
Waiting until **2031** to act would be waiting far too long.
think: With robots in **2034** I'm 66, so I nearly reach the state pension first.
Thinking AI in 2031 could still push Gwen to **cut my hours** before then.
do: Keep milking and add about **a hundred a month** to cover a year of reduced hours.
Go to the branch's **transition fund** meetings and vote for candidates who back it.
Ask Gwen to keep me **part-time with the calves** until I'm 67.
feel: **Anxious** but less frightened, like running for a bus I can still catch.
**Angry** on behalf of young workers like Kofi, who won't get out in time.
S3.quote: Our young farmhand Kofi is 24, and a robot would take his whole working life before he turns 32.
fieldNote: The **extra three years** nearly carry him to pension age, which softens fear but not anger.
Ines's **school cook job** is the household's steadying income in his mind.
His anger shifts to **young colleagues** once his own path looks just about safe.

steps.text: Keep doing the milking at Hollin Farm
Save an extra 100 a month to cover reduced hours
Attend transition fund meetings and vote for candidates backing it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so there's no excuse not to. At the branch I'd say we should be bargaining now for the young ones, because I'll be gone by then. And to friends at the pub I'd say, quite honestly, I'll be watching this one from my armchair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2039, I'm 71. I'll have been retired four years. It's not my fight for my own job any more, though the thinking AI in 2036 might shake up the farm when I'm 68 and probably out anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and stick to the plan: milk till 66 or 67, then stop. I'd keep going to the union branch and vote for parties that want a fair share of the robot money spread around. That's about it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose, but more for the grandkids than for me. It's a strange relief, being old enough to miss it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grandkids to learn something you do with your hands and your head together, like Tomas with his wiring. And to join a union from day one, even if their friends laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of you that would want to see the robots on Hollin Farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part of me, yes, if it meant Kofi didn't have to scrape yards in the sleet. If the robot does the dirty work and the people still get paid, I'm all for it, but I've never seen that happen.

say: **Ten years** is enough to do the change properly, so there's no excuse for doing it badly.
The union should bargain now for the **young workers**, because I'll be retired by then.
think: Robots in **2039** come four years after I've retired, so my job isn't at stake.
The **2036** thinking AI may shake up the farm, but I'd likely be gone by then.
do: Keep to the plan of milking until **66 or 67**, then stopping work at Hollin Farm.
Keep going to the **union branch** and vote for parties that share out the robot gains.
feel: **Uneasy** for the grandchildren, with an odd **relief** at being old enough to miss it.
S4.quote: If the robot does the dirty work and the people still get paid, I'm all for it, but I've never seen that happen.
fieldNote: With a **decade's warning** his own job drops out of the picture; worry moves to family.
He's not against robots in principle; he objects to the **gains not being shared**.
His advice to grandchildren mixes **trade skills** and union membership.

steps.text: Keep milking at Hollin Farm until 66 or 67
Vote for parties that would share out the robot gains

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. It puts the robots on the yard when I'm 63 and there's nothing in between me and the state pension. What would help is a pension bridge for older farmworkers, paid from the money the robots save, and a union that's at the table before the machines arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Everyone asks if the robots are coming, but nobody asks who gets the money when they do. That's the only question that matters to a man who's already lost one job to a closing.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if the robots are coming, but nobody asks who gets the money when they do.
portrait: Rafael is a **58-year-old milker** at Hollin Farm, four years in after the paper mill where he was shop steward closed.
He frames every scenario in terms of **ownership and pay**, and turns to the union rather than personal reinvention.
He never uses **AI tools** and has no plan to start; he'd rather fight for terms than learn the machine.
His mood rises from uneasy to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, then eases as the warning time pushes robots past his pension.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would reach the milking parlour when he's 63, four years short of his pension.
whatWouldHelp: A **pension bridge** for older farmworkers paid from robot savings, and a union at the table **before** machines arrive.
